source_text: Δημιουργὸν τῶν πάντων τιθέμενος αὐτὸν τὸ τοῦ Λόγου ὄνομα κατηγορεῖ αὐτοῦ. ἐπεὶ γὰρ ὡς ἐπίπαν πᾶσα δημιουργία ἤρτηται λόγου, οὐκ ἄλλως ἔδει αὐτὸν τῶν πάντων δηλῶσαι ὄντα ποιητὴν ἔχουσιν (αὕτη δέ ἐστιν ἕξις μετὰ ἀδόλου λόγου ποιητική), ὁ δὲ τοῦ θεοῦ υἱός, οὐκ ἄλλος ὢς ἢ σοφίας καὶ τέχνης δημιουργός, εἰκότως λόγος ὀνομάζεται. οὐ γὰρ ἄλλη τις ὢν οὐσία παρὰ τὸν λόγου δι᾿ αὐτοῦ ποιεὶ τὰ ὄντα, ἀλλ᾿ αὐτός ἐστιν ὁ ποιῶν, θεὸς ὢν λόγος. εἶτ᾿ ἐπεὶ ὁ λόγος οὗτος, θεὸς ὢν κατ’ οὐσίαν καὶ αὐτὸ τοῦτο θεοῦ υἱὸς ὑπάρχων, τῆς τῶν ἀνθρώπων σωτηρίας χάριν ἄνθρωπος γεγένηται, »Σὰρξ« ὁ λόγος ὠνομάσθη. καὶ ἐπεί τινες τῆς ὀρθῆς πίστεως ἐκπεσόντες οἴονται ἀπὸ τότε αὐτὸν μόνον εἶναι ἀφ’ οὑ ἐκ τῆς παρθένου ἄνθρωπος γεγονὼς προῆλθεν, ὀρθότατα πρὸς τοὺς τοιούτους ὁ θεολόγος γράφει τὸ »Ἐν ἀρχῇ ἦν ὁ λόγος« καὶ καταλλήλως τοῖς ῥήμασι χρησάμενος, τῷ μὲν »Ἐγένετο« ἐπὶ τῆς σαρκὸς, τῷ δὲ »Ἦν« ἐπὶ τῆς θεότητος αὐτοῦ σημαίνει]. καὶ ἦν μὲν κυριώτερον ἐπὶ τοῦ θεοῦ λόγου τὸ »Ἔστιν« εἰπεῖν· ἀλλ᾿ ἐπεὶ πρὸς διαφορὰν τῆς ἐνανθρωπήσεως γενομένης ἔν τινι καιρῷ ἐδήλου τὴν ὓπαρξιν τοῦ λόγου, ἀντὶ τοῦ »Ἔστιν« τῷ »Ἦν« ὁ εὐαγγελιστὴς κέχρηται. τῶν δὲ ῥημάτων τὰς κυρίας σημασίας ἐκλαμβάνειν οὐ δεῖ ἐπὶ τῶν ἀιδίων· ὅτε μὲν γὰρ τὰ σημαινόμενα ὑπὸ τούτων χρόνῳ συμμετρουμένην ἔχει τὴν ὕπαρξιν, ὡς τὸ Ἦν τὸ μηκέτ’ ὄν, ἀλλά ποτε ὁμοίως τὸ Ἔστι δηλοῖ τὸ νῦν ὑπάρχον, ὡς τὸ Ἔσται τὸ μέλλον ὑπάρξαι]]. ἀλλ᾿ ἐπεὶ ὁ λόγος τοῦ θεοῦ ἀίδιός ἐστι, τυγχάνων θεός, τὰ ῥήματα ἐπ᾿ αὐτοῦ οὐ μετὰ τοῦ προσσημαίνειν χρόνον ἐκλαμβάνειν δεῖ, τοῦ σημαινομένου ὑπ᾿ αὐτῶν οὐχ ὑπὸ χρόνον ὄντος. ἔστι δὲ ἀπ᾿ αὐτῶν τῶν τοῦ θεολόγου φωνῶν θηρεῦσαι τὴν διάνοιαν. εὐθὺς γὰρ ἀρχόμενος τῆς κατ’ αὐτὸν συντάξεως, γράφει· »Ἐν »Ἐν ἀρχῇ ἦν ὁ λόγος( ἦν γὰρ ἐν ἀρχῇ ποιῶν τὸν οὐρανὸν καὶ τὴν γῆν. εἰ γὰρ »Πάντα δι’ αὐτοῦ ἐγένετο«, τῶν πάντων δὲ ὁ οὐρανὸς καὶ ἡ γῆ ὑπῆρχεν, ἐν τῇ τούτων οὐσιώσει αὐτὸς ἠν κτίστης αὐτῶν. εἶτ᾿ ἐπεὶ μὴ εἶπεν έν τῇ τινὸς ἀρχῇ ὁ λόγος ἦν, καθόλου ληπτέον αὐτό, ἕν’ ᾖ τὸ δηλούμενον τοιοῦτον· έν ἀρχῇ τῶν ἀγγέλων, καὶ ἐν ἀρχῇ τῶν ἀρχαγγέλων ἦν ὁ λόγος· καὶ συνελόντι εἰπεῖν, ἐν ἀρχῇ τῶν ὁρατῶν τε καὶ ἀοράτων κτισμάτων ἦν ὁ λόγος, πάντων αὐτῶν ὢν ἀρχὴ τε καὶ ποιητής. ἐν Χριστῷ γὰρ »ἐκτίσθη τὰ πάντα«, τά τε »ἐν τοῖς οὐρανοῖς καὶ τὰ ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς, τά τε ὀρατὰ καὶ τὰ ἀόρατα, »εἴτε ἀρχαὶ εἴτε ἐξουσίαι εἴτε θρόνοι εἴτε κυριότητες· πάντα δι᾿ αὐτοῦ καὶ εἰς αὐτὸν ἐκτισται· καὶ αὐτός ἐστι πρὸ πάντων καὶ τὰ πάντα έν αὐτῷ συνέστηκεν, ὅς ἐστιν ἀρχὴ, πρωτότοκος ἐκ τῶν νεκρῶν( εἰ γὰρ τὰ πάντα έν αὐτῷ συνέστηκεν, καὶ πρὸ αὐτῶν ἐστιν, ἀρχὴ αὐτῶν κατὰ τὸ εἶναι αἴτιος ὑπάρχων, ἀκολούθως ῥητέον εἶναι αὐτὸν ἐν τῇ πάντων οὐσιώσει. πῶς γὰρ οὐκ ἔδει αὐτὸν εἶναι πρὸ αὐτῶν καὶ ἐν ἀρχῇ τῆς ὑπάρξεως αὐτῶν κτίστην ὄντα; εἶτ᾿ ἐπεὶ ἐν ἀρχῇ αὐτὸν εἶπεν εἶναι ἔδει δηλῶσαι καὶ πῶς καὶ πρὸς τίνα ὄντα ποιεῖν αὐτὸν ἐχρῆν. διὸ ἐπήγαγεν τῷ »Ἐν τῇ ἀρχῇ ἦν »Ὁ λόγος« καὶ τὸ »Ἧν ὁ λόγος πρὸς τὸν θεόν«· πρὸς ἡμᾶς μὲν γὰρ ἐλθών, ὅτε ἐκ παρθένου ἐτέχθη, ἀπέσταλτο ὑπὸ τοῦ πατρός·
pass_a_gloss: Positing him maker of all things, he predicates of him the name of the Word. For since on the whole every making hangs on a word (reason), it was not necessary to show him maker of all otherwise, in those having [art] (and this is a habit productive with guileless reason); and the Son of God, being none other than craftsman of wisdom and art, is fittingly named Word. For not being some other substance beside the Word does he make the beings through it, but he himself is the one making, being God Word. Then since this Word, being God according to substance and being this very thing, Son of God, became man for the sake of the salvation of men, the Word was named Flesh. And since some, having fallen out of the right faith, suppose him to exist only from then, from when, having become man from the virgin, he came forth, most rightly toward such the theologian writes the In beginning was the Word; and using the verbs correspondingly, by Became he signifies about the flesh, and by Was about his deity. And it would have been more proper to say Is of the God Word; but since he was making plain the existence of the Word toward a distinction from the becoming-man which happened at a certain time, instead of Is the evangelist has used Was. One must not take the proper meanings of the verbs in the case of the eternal things; for when the things signified by these have an existence measured together with time, as Was the no-longer-being but once-being, likewise Is makes plain the now-existing, as Will be the about-to-exist. But since the Word of God is eternal, being God, one must not take the verbs of him with co-signifying time, the thing signified by them not being under time. It is possible to hunt the meaning from the very utterances of the theologian. For straightway beginning his composition he writes: In beginning was the Word; for he was in the beginning making the heaven and the earth. For if All things came to be through him, and of all things heaven and earth were, in their being brought into substance he was their creator. Then since he did not say in the beginning of something was the Word, it must be taken universally, so that what is shown is such: in beginning of the angels and in beginning of the archangels was the Word; and to speak summarily, in beginning of the visible and invisible creatures was the Word, being of all of them both beginning and maker. For in Christ were created all things, those in the heavens and those on the earth, the visible and the invisible, whether rulers or authorities or thrones or lordships; all things have been created through him and into him; and he is before all things and all things stand together in him, who is beginning, firstborn from the dead. For if all things stand together in him, and he is before them, being their beginning as cause according to being, consequently one must say he is in the bringing into substance of all. For how was it not necessary that he be before them and in the beginning of their existence, being creator? Then since he said he was in beginning, it was necessary to show also how and toward whom being he had to make. Therefore he added to In the beginning was the Word also The Word was toward God; for having come toward us, when he was born from a virgin, he had been sent by the Father.
pass_b_english: Since he presents him as the maker of all things, he gives him the name “Word”. For as a rule every act of making depends on a word, that is, on reason, in those who have [art]; and art is a habit of making joined with reason free of deceit. So there was no other way to show that he is the maker of all things. And the Son of God, being nothing other than the craftsman of wisdom and art, is fittingly named Word. For he is not some substance other than the Word, making existing things through a word; he himself is the maker, being God the Word.

Then, since this Word, being God by substance and being this very thing, the Son of God, became man for the sake of human salvation, the Word was named “flesh” (John 1:14). And since some, who have fallen away from the right faith, think that he exists only from the time when he came forth from the virgin, having become man, the theologian writes most rightly against such people: “In the beginning was the Word” (John 1:1). And he uses the verbs fittingly: by “became” he signifies his flesh, and by “was” his Godhead.

It would indeed have been more proper to say “is” of God the Word. But since he was showing the existence of the Word in distinction from the incarnation, which took place at a certain time, the evangelist used “was” instead of “is”. Yet with eternal things we must not take the verbs in their proper meanings. When the things they signify have an existence measured by time, “was” signifies what no longer is but once was; so too “is” shows what exists now, and “will be” what is going to exist. But since the Word of God is eternal, being God, the verbs used of him must not be taken as also signifying time, for what they signify is not under time.

One can track down the meaning from the theologian's own words. For right at the start of his treatise he writes: “In the beginning was the Word”; for in the beginning he was making the heaven and the earth (Genesis 1:1). If “all things were made through him” (John 1:3), and heaven and earth were among all things, then he was their creator when they came into being. Then, since he did not say, “In the beginning of something was the Word”, the phrase must be taken universally, so that the meaning is this: In the beginning of the angels, and in the beginning of the archangels, was the Word; in short, in the beginning of the creatures visible and invisible was the Word, being of them all both beginning and maker.

For in Christ “all things were created, things in the heavens and things on earth, visible and invisible, whether principalities or powers or thrones or dominions: all things were created through him and for him; and he is before all things, and in him all things hold together; who is the beginning, the firstborn from the dead” (Colossians 1:16-18). If all things hold together in him, and he is before them, being their beginning as the cause of their existence, it follows that we must say he was there when all things came into being. For how could he, their creator, not have had to be before them and at the beginning of their existence? Then, since he said that he was in the beginning, he had to show both how he was, and with whom he was when he was to make. So to “In the beginning was the Word” he added “and the Word was with God” (John 1:1). For when he came to us, when he was born of the virgin, he had been sent by the Father.

choices.choice: 2026-11-11 round 2: the justification still held a September one-sentence summary as Pass B. The published English was close, but it ended '[the fragment breaks off]' where the source block had only been cut; the block now continues to the start of john-catena-2 and is translated.

'οὐκ ἄλλως ἔδει αὐτὸν τῶν πάντων δηλῶσαι ὄντα ποιητὴν ἔχουσιν' lacks a word; '[art]' is supplied in brackets from the parenthesis, which defines art (Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics 6.4: a productive habit with true reason).

choices.why: the argument plays on word and reason; both are given once, then 'Word'

choices.choice: The digital text keeps the edition's closing brackets ']' after σημαίνει and ']]' after ὑπάρξαι without their opening marks; they are left in the Greek and not shown in the English.
ὢς read ὢν; λόγου (after παρὰ τὸν) read λόγον; ἠν read ἦν; 'Ἐν »Ἐν' doubled word read once; έν read ἐν; ὀρατὰ read ὁρατὰ; ἕν’ ᾖ read ἵν’ ᾖ.
